L225: ```powershell
L226: Test-UI 'Keyboard save' {
L227:     Invoke-Ui @('send-keys', 'hello world', '--target', 'TxtName', '--via', 'send-input')
L228:     Invoke-Ui @('send-keys', 'ctrl+s', '--via', 'send-input')
L229:     Invoke-Ui @('wait-for', 'StatusBar', '--value', 'saved', '--contains', '-t', '2000')
L230: }
L231: Test-UI 'Tooltip' {
L232:     Invoke-Ui @('hover', 'BtnInfo')
L233:     Invoke-Ui @('wait-for', 'InfoTooltip', '-t', '2000')
L234: }
L235: Test-UI 'Reorder items' {
L236:     Invoke-Ui @('drag', 'ItemA', 'ItemB')
L237:     Invoke-Ui @('wait-for', 'StatusBar', '--value', 'reordered', '--contains', '-t', '2000')
L238: }
L239: Test-UI 'Touch and ink input' {
L240:     Invoke-Ui @('touch', 'LstFeed', '-g', 'swipe', '--direction', 'up', '--distance', '400')
L241:     Invoke-Ui @('pen', 'InkCanvas', '--path', '50,50 120,80 200,60', '--pressure', '0.8')
L242:     Save-Screenshot '03-ink.png'
L243:     # Add the app-specific state assertion; successful injection alone is not functional proof.
L244: }
L245: ```
L246: Use `winapp ui drag --help`, `winapp ui touch --help`, and `winapp ui pen --help` for coordinates, long-press/dwell, pinch/stretch, pressure/tilt/eraser support. Read coordinates in the guest tree; host coordinates are not guest coordinates.
L247: ### Recordings and workflow coordination
L248: 
L249: ```powershell
L250: Test-UI 'Video delivered' {
L251:     $video = Join-Path $ArtifactDirectory 'flow.mp4'
L252:     if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $video) { throw 'Choose a new video evidence path.' }
L253:     Invoke-Ui @('record', '--duration-sec', '6', '--fps', '30', '--output', $video)
L254:     if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $video -PathType Leaf) -or (Get-Item -LiteralPath $video).Length -eq 0) {
L255:         throw "Recording was not delivered to the host: $video"
L256:     }
L257: }
L258: ```
L259: Sandbox screenshot/record **`--output` paths are host paths**, automatically delivered when capture completes; do not pull them from guessed guest directories. Use fresh output paths and check the exit status and actual host files. `--capture-screen` can include popups outside the app window. For an interrupted recording, preserve `stopReason`, `partialOutput`, `recoveryHint`, and the reported partial/recovery paths; a nonempty partial file is not necessarily playable.
L260: WinApp CLI arbitrates desktop-changing commands automatically. Without a workflow ID, each command releases its turn immediately; with one, the four-second grace covers tight script bursts, not agent reasoning. Use the **same `WINAPP_UI_WORKFLOW_ID`** for cooperating commands, including concurrent recording and interaction; independent flows need distinct IDs.
L261: The template accepts `-WorkflowId` for this purpose, sets it in its own process, restores the previous value, and calls `winapp ui yield --on sandbox` in `finally`. Fresh shell tool calls do not inherit changes from an earlier shell: set the same ID on **every** cooperating invocation. A separate concurrent recording process must also check its exit code/delivery, use the same scoped PID, and finish before the test runner yields.
L262: Do not start an independent-ID recording that blocks the interactions it is meant to capture. After a pause, inspect again and reopen menus/dialogs another workflow may have changed.
L263: ### Guest persistence and arbitrary file transfer
L264: 
L265: Do not inspect **host** `$env:LOCALAPPDATA` to prove **guest** persistence. Check the actual app data file in the selected target. Replace the sample package family/path with the app's real storage location; unpackaged apps usually use an app-specific LocalAppData directory.
L266: ```powershell
L267: Test-UI 'Username persisted in selected target' {
L268:     $readSettings = @'
L269: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
L270: $file = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA 'Packages\YourPackageFamily\LocalState\settings.json'
L271: if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $file -PathType Leaf)) { throw "Missing settings: $file" }
L272: Get-Content -LiteralPath $file -Raw
L273: '@
L274:     $json = if ($Target -eq 'sandbox') {
L275:         Invoke-WinAppChecked @('target', 'exec', 'sandbox', '--', 'powershell.exe', '-NoProfile', '-NonInteractive', '-Command', $readSettings)
L276:     } else {
L277:         & ([scriptblock]::Create($readSettings))
L278:     }
L279:     $settings = $json | ConvertFrom-Json
L280:     if ($settings.UserName -ne 'TestUser') { throw 'Saved username does not match.' }
L281: }
L282: ```
L283: For arbitrary setup/results files, use `target exec` / `push` / `pull`, not host filesystem guesses. Transfer guest paths are **relative to snapshot `workRoot`**, normally `C:\WinApp\work`, not absolute guest paths. The following optional additions assume a host `setup.ps1` that creates `Results` under the guest work root:
L284: ```powershell
L285: Test-UI 'Guest setup and result transfer' {
L286:     if ($Target -ne 'sandbox') { throw 'This transfer test requires Sandbox.' }
L287:     $snapshot = Invoke-WinAppChecked @('target', 'snapshot', 'sandbox', '--json') | ConvertFrom-Json
L288:     if (-not $snapshot.workRoot) { throw 'No live guest workRoot; fix readiness first.' }
L289:     Invoke-WinAppChecked @('target', 'push', 'sandbox', '.\setup.ps1', 'Setup\setup.ps1')
L290:     $guestSetup = $snapshot.workRoot.TrimEnd('\') + '\Setup\setup.ps1'
L291:     Invoke-WinAppChecked @('target', 'exec', 'sandbox', '--', 'powershell.exe', '-NoProfile', '-File', $guestSetup)
L292:     Invoke-WinAppChecked @('target', 'pull', 'sandbox', 'Results', (Join-Path $ArtifactDirectory 'results'))
L293: }
L294: ```
L295: Keep the guest alive while recovering failed delivery. Preserve evidence/recovery paths and app data needed for diagnosis before any **user-consented** shutdown; never stop all Sandboxes as routine cleanup.
L296: ### Binding and selector gotchas
L297: - `set-value` does not commit default WinUI `x:Bind TwoWay` TextBox bindings until focus changes. Prefer `UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged` in the app; otherwise `invoke` Save or `focus` another control before checking persistence.
L298: - RichEditBox/RichTextBox generally need `send-keys --via send-input`, not UIA `set-value`.
L299: - Use `$AppPid`, never PowerShell's read-only automatic `$Pid`.
L300: - A picker HWND needs `-w` **and the same target scope**. A fresh guest invalidates both HWNDs and PIDs; do not recycle either.

L2: priority: HIGH

L4: sources:
L5:   - https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/apps/design/basics/navigation-basics
L6:   - https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/apps/design/basics/titlebar-design
L7:   - https://github.com/microsoft/WinUI-Gallery
L8:   - https://github.com/microsoft/WindowsAppSDK-Samples/tree/main/Samples/Windowing
L9: ---
L10: ## What This Reference Is For
L11: 
L12: Use this file for top-level app shells, page navigation models, custom title bars, and multi-window decisions.
L13: 
L14: ## Prefer
L15: 
L16: - `NavigationView` for standard desktop shells with clear top-level destinations.
L17: - A small, stable set of primary destinations.
L18: - Built-in back navigation behavior that matches user expectations.
L19: - `AppWindow` and Windows App SDK windowing APIs for modern window management.
L20: ## Avoid
L21: 
L22: - Overloading the nav surface with every command and secondary action.
L23: - Turning the `NavigationView` pane into a branded hero area when the user did not ask for custom shell treatment.
L24: - Custom title bar layouts that break drag regions or caption button clarity.
L25: - Multi-window designs unless the workflow clearly benefits from them.
L26: ## Navigation Guidance
L27: - Use left navigation when the app has several stable, high-level destinations.
L28: - Use top navigation when there are few peer destinations and width is available.
L29: - Use a single-page or document-first layout when navigation is shallow and the user mostly stays in one workflow.
L30: - Keep naming and iconography stable across pages.
L31: - Treat `NavigationView` as functional shell chrome first. Keep pane headers, footer content, and decorative branding minimal unless the product requirements clearly call for them.
L32: - Prefer the platform's normal pane structure before adding custom logo blocks, taglines, or non-navigation content that changes the shell's native feel.
L33: - For narrow or phone-like widths, stop reserving permanent pane width for desktop navigation. Prefer a minimal or overlay navigation mode, show the pane toggle when needed, close the pane by default after navigation, and give content the width back.
L34: - When a shell enters a phone-width mode, reduce content padding and decorative chrome so the page reads as one primary column instead of a desktop shell with a squeezed content strip.
L35: ## Title Bar Guidance
L36: 
L37: - Treat the title bar as functional chrome first, branding surface second.
L38: - Keep empty non-interactive areas draggable.
L39: - Blend title bar visuals with the rest of the app when possible.
L40: - Respect light, dark, and high-contrast states.
L41: ## Windowing Guidance
L42: 
L43: - Start with one main window.
L44: - Add secondary windows only for workflows such as document detachment, inspection panes, or tool windows.
L45: - Use Windows App SDK samples for resizing, placement, and window-specific behaviors instead of inventing custom platform abstractions.
L46: 
L47: ## Sample and Source Anchors
L48: 
L49: - WinUI Gallery `NavigationView`, `TitleBar`, `AppWindow`, and windowing sample pages
L50: - WindowsAppSDK-Samples `Samples/Windowing`
L51: - Learn navigation and title bar guidance
L52: ## Review Checklist
L53: 
L54: - Is the navigation model simple and intentional?
L55: - Does the shell still look and behave like a normal WinUI `NavigationView` unless there is an explicit reason to diverge?
L56: - Does the title bar still behave like a Windows title bar?
L57: - Are back, search, and pane behaviors consistent?
L58: - Is multi-window use justified by the workflow?
L59: - Does the shell intentionally switch behavior at narrow or phone widths instead of leaving a full desktop pane open?

L6: # Installation【1†】
L7: ## Packages【2†】
L8: 
L9: Note that if at any point the package you’re trying to use is outdated, you always have the option to use an official binary from the restic project.
L10: 
L11: These are up to date binaries, built in a reproducible and verifiable way, that you can download and run without having to do additional installation work.
L12: 
L13: Please see the 【3†Official binaries】 section below for various downloads. Official binaries can be updated in place by using the `restic self-update` command.
L14: The environment variable `$GITHUB_ACCESS_TOKEN` can be set to use a personal access token when updating. This increases the rate limit through authenticated GitHub API requests, and prevents update failures when many unauthenticated requests have already been made from the same IP.
L15: ### Alpine Linux【4†】
L16: 
L17: On 【5†Alpine Linux†www.alpinelinux.org】 you can install the `restic` package from the official community repos, e.g. using `apk`:
L18: 
L19:     $ apk add restic
L20: 
L21: 
L22: ### Arch Linux【6†】
L23: 
L24: On 【7†Arch Linux†archlinux.org】, you can install the `restic` package from the official community repos, e.g. with `pacman -S`:
L25: 
L26:     $ pacman -S restic
L27: ### Debian【8†】
L28: 
L29: On Debian, there’s a package called `restic` which can be installed from the official repos, e.g. with `apt-get`:
L30: 
L31:     $ apt-get install restic
L32: 
L33: 
L34: ### Fedora【9†】
L35: 
L36: restic can be installed using `dnf`:
L37: 
L38:     $ dnf install restic
L39: 
L40: 
L41: If you used restic from copr previously, remove the copr repo as follows to avoid any conflicts:
L42: 
L43:     $ dnf copr remove copart/restic
L44: ### Gentoo Linux【10†】
L45: 
L46: On 【11†Gentoo Linux†www.gentoo.org】, you can install the `restic` package from the official repos using `emerge`:
L47: 
L48:     # emerge restic
L49: 
L50: 
L51: ### macOS【12†】
L52: 
L53: If you are using macOS, you can install restic using 【13†Homebrew†brew.sh】:
L54: 
L55:     $ brew install restic
L56: 
L57: 
L58: On Linux and macOS, you can also install it using 【14†pkgx†pkgx.sh】:
L59: 
L60:     $ pkgx install restic
L61: 
L62: 
L63: You may also install it using 【15†MacPorts†www.macports.org】:
L64: 
L65:     $ sudo port install restic
L66: ### Nix & NixOS【16†】
L67: 
L68: If you are using 【17†Nix / NixOS†nixos.org】, there is a package named `restic` available in 【18†nixpkgs†search.nixos.org】. You can install it by adding this to your `configuration.nix`:
L69: 
L70:     environment.systemPackages = [
L71:       pkgs.restic
L72:     ];
L73: 
L74: 
L75: ### Mise (Linux/macOS/Windows)【19†】
L76: 
L77: If you are using 【20†Mise†mise.jdx.dev】, you can install `restic` using this command:
L78: 
L79:     $ mise use -g restic@latest
L80: ### OpenBSD【21†】
L81: 
L82: On OpenBSD 6.3 and greater, you can install restic using `pkg_add`:
L83: 
L84:     # pkg_add restic
L85: 
L86: 
L87: ### FreeBSD【22†】
L88: 
L89: On FreeBSD (11 and probably later versions), you can install restic using `pkg install`:
L90: 
L91:     # pkg install restic
L92: 
L93: 
L94: ### openSUSE【23†】
L95: 
L96: On openSUSE (leap 15.0 and greater, and tumbleweed), you can install restic using the `zypper` package manager:
L97: 
L98:     # zypper install restic
L99: ### RHEL & CentOS Stream【24†】
L100: 
L101: For supported RHEL / CentOS Stream releases, restic can be installed from the EPEL repository:
L102: 
L103:     $ dnf install epel-release
L104:     $ dnf install restic
L105: 
L106: 
L107: ### Solus【25†】
L108: 
L109: restic can be installed from the official repo of Solus via the `eopkg` package manager:
L110: 
L111:     $ eopkg install restic
L112: ### Windows【26†】
L113: 
L114: restic can be installed using either 【27†Scoop†scoop.sh】 or 【28†WinGet†learn.microsoft.com】.
L115: 
L116: Regardless of the method, the `restic.exe` binary will be added to your `PATH` automatically, making the `restic` command accessible in PowerShell or CMD.
L117: 
L118:     scoop install restic
L119: 
L120: 
L121:     winget install --exact --id restic.restic --scope Machine
L122: By default, WinGet will install restic into the `User` scope, which is typically in your user’s `%LOCALAPPDATA%` directory. This behavior may be undesirable for system-wide backups, so specifying `--scope Machine` is recommended so that restic is installed into `%ProgramFiles%`. This requires elevation.
L123: ## Official binaries【3†】
L124: ### Stable releases【29†】
L125: 
L126: You can download the latest stable release versions of restic from the 【30†restic release page†github.com】. These builds are considered stable and releases are made regularly in a controlled manner.
L127: 
L128: There are both pre-compiled binaries for different platforms as well as the source code available for download. Just download and run the one matching your system.
L129: On your first installation, if you desire, you can verify the integrity of your downloads by testing the SHA-256 checksums listed in `SHA256SUMS` and verifying the integrity of the file `SHA256SUMS` with the PGP signature in `SHA256SUMS.asc`. The PGP signature was created using the key (【31†0x91A6868BD3F7A907†restic.net】):
L130:

L132:           Key fingerprint = CF8F 18 F2 8445 7597 3 F79  D4E1 91 A6 868 B D3F7 A907

L134:           sub   4096 R/D5FC2ACF4043FDF1 2014-11-01
L135: Once downloaded, the official binaries can be updated in place using the `restic self-update` command (needs restic 0.9.3 or later):

L160: ### Unstable builds【32†】
L161: 
L162: Another option is to use the latest builds for the master branch, available on the 【33†restic beta download site†beta.restic.net】. These too are pre-compiled and ready to run, and a new version is built every time a push is made to the master branch.
L163: ## Docker container【34†】
L164: 
L165: A minimal Docker image with just a few files and the restic binary is available; you can get it with `docker pull` like this:
L166: 
L167:     $ docker pull restic/restic
L168: 
L169: 
L170: The container is also available on the GitHub Container Registry:
L171: 
L172:     $ docker pull ghcr.io/restic/restic
L173: Restic relies on the hostname for various operations. Make sure to set a static hostname using `--hostname` when creating a Docker container, otherwise Docker will assign a random hostname each time.
L174: 
L175: The container additionally honors traditional `nice` 【35†(man page)†man7.org】 and `ionice` 【36†(man page)†man7.org】 directives via the following environment variables. This allows restic to be scheduled as a background process to reduce latency for the system while running.
L176:   * `NICE`: If set, this adjusts the CPU prioritization via `nice -n`. This defaults to no adjustment - standard CPU priority.
L177: 
L178:   * `IONICE_CLASS`: If set, this adjusts the IO prioritization of the restic process via `ionice -c` for the available classes. Note: if you attempt to set real-time, you will have to add the `SYS_NICE` capability (【37†see capabilities manpage†man7.org】) to allow using this IO class.
L179:   * `IONICE_PRIORITY`: This defaults to 4 (no prioritization or penalties); this is the prioritization within the given `IONICE_CLASS`.
L180: 
L181: The following example runs restic such that other CPU and IO requests have higher priority. This effectively perturbs the system as minimally as possible while `restic` runs.
L182: 
L183:     # docker run -e NICE=20 -e IONICE_CLASS=2 -e IONICE_PRIORITY=7 ghcr.io/restic/restic
L184: Remember that this invocation is explicitly telling your CPU and IO scheduler to deprioritize restic. This typically will result in a longer runtime. For a system with heavy load, this can be drastically longer.
L185: ## From source【38†】
L186: 
L187: restic is written in the Go programming language and you need at least Go version 1.25. Building restic may also work with older versions of Go, but that’s not supported. See the 【39†Getting started†go.dev】 guide of the Go project for instructions how to install Go.
L188: 
L189: In order to build restic from source, execute the following steps:
L190: 
L191:     $ git clone https://github.com/restic/restic
L192:     [...]
L193: 
L194:     $ cd restic
L195: 
L196:     $ go run build.go
L197: You can easily cross-compile restic for all supported platforms, just supply the target OS and platform via the command-line options like this (for Windows and FreeBSD respectively):
L198: 
L199:     $ go run build.go --goos windows --goarch amd64
L200: 
L201:     $ go run build.go --goos freebsd --goarch 386
L202: 
L203:     $ go run build.go --goos linux --goarch arm --goarm 6
L204: 
L205:     $ go run build.go --goos solaris --goarch amd64
L206: 
L207: 
L208: The resulting binary is statically linked and does not require any libraries.
L209: At the moment, the only tested compiler for restic is the official Go compiler. Building restic with gccgo may work, but is not supported.
L210: ## Autocompletion【40†】
L211: Restic can write out man pages and bash/fish/zsh/powershell compatible autocompletion scripts:
L212: 
L213:     $ ./restic generate --help
L214: 
L215:     The "generate" command writes automatically generated files (like the man pages
L216:     and the auto-completion files for bash, fish, powershell and zsh).
